Maintaining Deep-Learning Surrogate Accuracy for Long-Term Groundwater Remediation:

w:r.w:delText: Deep-learning surrogate models can reduce groundwater simulation times from hours or days to seconds, making it feasible to rapidly evaluate remediation alternatives, explore uncertainty, and support planning decisions that would otherwise be constrained by computational cost. For U.S. Department of Energy
Office of Environmental Management (EM) sites managing complex, long-duration groundwater cleanup, this capability offers substantial operational value.

However, surrogate models are trained on data that represent site conditions at a particular point in time. Over the years and decades typical of EM remediation, those conditions may change because of natural system evolution, modifications to pumping or treatment systems, new monitoring data, or revisions to the conceptual site model. As a result, surrogate accuracy may degrade over time. If such degradation is not detected and addressed, surrogate-informed decisions may no longer be reliable. In regulatory settings governed by
Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act
and DOE quality assurance requirements, that risk is unacceptable.

Although interest in surrogate modeling is growing within the environmental modeling community, no established methodology currently exists for maintaining surrogate accuracy over multi-year operational periods while preserving the governance, documentation, and quality assurance standards required for EM applications.

Monitoring and evidence-based review are needed to determine whether it remains suitable for use.

This report connects model maintenance to the governance and quality assurance expectations of environmental decision support: when to intervene, how to assess an update, and what evidence permits deployment.

This revised report develops that process through a three-pillar framework and a controlled pump-and-treat U-Net case study. The central questions are when an update is warranted, how the update can preserve useful historical behavior, and what evidence is required before the candidate may be used. w:r.w:t: Deep-learning (DL) surrogates can accelerate groundwater flow and transport predictions, making large scenario sets and uncertainty analyses more practical. Their reliability can change as pumping systems, source conditions, boundary conditions, or conceptual models change. This report connects a governance-aware framework for managing those changes to a controlled U-Net update case study for pump-and-treat plume prediction. The intended role remains screening, scenario exploration, and planning support within DOE environmental management.

Within this framework, surrogate models are explicitly limited to screening-level analyses, scenario exploration, and planning support. High-fidelity physics-based models remain the authoritative basis for final regulatory and remedy decisions. When surrogate validity is in question, governance procedures require withdrawal of surrogate use and escalation to a controlled retraining process, thereby preventing unmanaged risk. This conservative posture is consistent with CERCLA protectiveness expectations and DOE quality assurance requirements.

The framework has four objectives. First, it defines a governance structure that aligns surrogate deployment and maintenance with established regulatory and quality assurance requirements. Second, it establishes systematic methods for monitoring surrogate performance and detecting degradation before decision support is compromised. Third, it provides efficient recalibration procedures to restore surrogate accuracy within predefined acceptance criteria while minimizing the burden of new high-fidelity simulations. Fourth, it operationalizes these capabilities through a structured workflow with explicit decision points, documentation requirements, and configuration control to support auditability, reproducibility, and independent review.

w:r.w:delText: These objectives are implemented through a seven-step, two-phase workflow. The first phase, continuous monitoring, runs during routine surrogate operation and includes monitoring performance indicators, detecting potential drift, and determining whether observed changes warrant action. The second phase, triggered response, is activated only when monitoring indicates meaningful degradation and governance review approves an update. It includes preparing new training data, updating surrogate parameters, validating the revised model against predefined acceptance criteria, and deploying the approved version under formal configuration control. Throughout this process, governance records document trigger rationale, data provenance, validation results, and deployment decisions to support transparency and auditability.

The report describes the methods underlying each pillar, including governance procedures aligned with EPA and DOE quality assurance standards, surrogate and physics-model architectures, and recalibration techniques drawn from the continual-learning and concept-drift literature. It also presents an implementation roadmap and a prototype demonstration plan featuring two proof-of-concept applications: a Fourier
perator surrogate for two-dimensional cross-section transport and a
plume prediction. These demonstrations are designed to test the complete recalibration cycle under controlled synthetic drift conditions.

This work makes three main contributions. First, it proposes a structured, governance-aware approach for maintaining surrogate models over long operational periods, addressing a gap in both the machine-learning and environmental-modeling literature. Second, it integrates uncertainty quantification, drift detection, and continual learning into a single operational workflow rather than treating them as isolated technical methods. Third, it establishes a governance template for applying adaptive machine-learning models in regulatory contexts, helping address a major barrier to operational adoption at EM sites.

The framework remains at the concept and design stage. Current limitations include dependence on the quality of the underlying physics-based models, the computational cost of some uncertainty quantification methods, and the need for validation under real field conditions with measurement noise, data gaps, and site complexity representative of EM applications. Prototype development and testing on representative groundwater remediation problems are the next steps toward eventual operational deployment.

w:r.w:t: The workflow has seven distinct steps. MONITOR collects performance and uncertainty evidence; DETECT evaluates possible degradation; DECIDE records the human judgment that an update is warranted. PREPARE assembles traceable data; UPDATE produces a candidate; CALIBRATE assesses and adjusts its predictive uncertainty; DEPLOY applies an independent final test and records the promotion decision. These are framework requirements, and the case study explicitly identifies which requirements have evidence and which remain to be demonstrated.

The case study uses reported U-Net/adaptive-replay results to examine rare-regime recovery and historical retention. Mass90 response changes define a retrospective stress condition, and reported update comparisons quantify the resulting tradeoff. An illustrative decision screen retains selected controller outcomes for further evaluation. No interval-calibration or final-promotion artifact is available, so the supported endpoint is a candidate awaiting calibration and final validation.

The report makes three connected contributions: a three-pillar governance and methods framework, a quantitative offline update case study mapped to its seven steps, and a concrete evidence specification for advancing toward an operational demonstration. The contribution is the connection between measured performance, decision criteria, and the next required evidence.

The current maturity is a defined framework with controlled update evidence. Prospective detector performance, independent uncertainty calibration, final-test promotion, and long-duration use with field data remain unverified. Physics-model limitations, data independence, measurement noise, irregular sampling, and operational complexity must be addressed as the framework progresses. The roadmap prioritizes those gaps while preserving human decision authority.

Deep learning surrogate models are AI

enabled, data-driven approximations of complex physical, numerical, or computational models, built using deep neural networks to emulate the behavior of high-fidelity simulations. Instead of repeatedly running computationally expensive models (e.g., groundwater flow, contaminant transport, or reactive chemistry), a surrogate model is trained on simulation or observational data to learn the input–output relationships and then provide rapid predictions.

These models are particularly valuable for tasks like uncertainty quantification, optimization, and real-time decision support, where thousands to millions of model evaluations may be required. By significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining acceptable accuracy, deep
learning surrogates enable faster scenario analysis, integration into AI-driven workflows, and scalable system-level optimization.

While surrogate models offer significant improvements in computational efficiency, they—like purely physics-based models—must still be rigorously verified, calibrated, and continuously updated as new data become available.

A surrogate trained at a single point in time encodes the conditions, parameters, and conceptual understanding reflected in its training data. As site conditions change — through natural system evolution, operational modifications, updated boundary conditions, or revised parameter estimates — the surrogate

s training distribution diverges from the conditions it is asked to predict. This divergence, termed distribution shift or concept drift, causes surrogate accuracy to degrade progressively. Without systematic detection and correction, this degradation can proceed silently, producing predictions that appear reasonable but are no longer reliable.

The physical phenomena represented typically include advection and dispersion of dissolved species, sorption onto solid phases, and associated reaction processes (

Genuchten 2016; Sethi and Di Molfetta 2019), and non-Fickian plume spreading arising from heterogeneity and diffusion-controlled mass exchange between transmissive and low-permeability zones (Guo et al. 2021). Back diffusion from fine

Engineered operations – pump and treat (P&T) wells, injection/extraction networks, permeable reactive barriers, and hydraulic barriers – must also be represented, enabling planners to evaluate how alternative configurations and engineered controls affect plume pathways and concentrations at compliance points.

Across the five families, several training practices recur in literature. Training datasets are generated by sampling parameter and boundary condition ranges, commonly using Latin hypercube or quasi-random designs, and running the corresponding high-fidelity simulations to produce input-output pairs (Asher et al. 2015; Razavi et al. 2012). The number of simulations required varies by problem complexity and surrogate architecture but generally falls in the range of hundreds to low thousands of realizations (Mo et al.

The drift monitoring framework consists of
complementary metrics organized into four categories (

). By combining complementary signals that capture loss of dynamical stability, increasing model uncertainty, and structural changes in data and learned representations, the framework allows early, interpretable, and statistically robust detection of regime drift to support timely model recalibration.

early signs of loss of dynamical stability, motivated by concepts from tipping point science. They are applied to model outputs, residuals, and latent representations, without implying the existence of physical tipping points in the underlying system. Rolling-window estimates of variance and lag-1 autocorrelation are used to detect increasing fluctuation amplitude and memory, consistent with reduced resilience. Higher-order moments, including skewness and kurtosis, are monitored to identify asymmetric error growth and heavy-tailed behavior indicative of excursions toward unstable regions.

These metrics focus on direct indicators of model reliability under deployment. Prediction residuals are monitored using adaptive thresholds derived from rolling statistics, such as exceedance of multiples of the rolling standard deviation. Persistent threshold violations or clustered spatial–temporal error patterns are treated as evidence of localized or systemic degradation.

For probabilistic models, predictive uncertainty is explicitly tracked using measures such as variance or entropy. Sustained increases relative to historical baselines are interpreted as growing epistemic uncertainty and declining confidence in model predictions.
These diagnostics target statistical and structural changes in data and learned features that may not immediately manifest in errors or uncertainty

Distributional drift is assessed by comparing incoming input and output distributions to reference distributions using nonparametric statistical tests, such as the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Statistically significant deviations indicate changes in the data-generating process that may compromise model validity.

In parallel, drift indicators are applied in learned representation spaces, such as latent embeddings from diffusion models or bottleneck features from convolutional architectures. Deviations from the training manifold in latent space provide early detection of regime mismatch in high-dimensional settings where marginal statistics may be insufficient.

The final category integrates all diagnostic signals into a robust decision-making layer. Rather than relying on single-metric thresholds, the framework employs Bayesian inference to combine evidence from resilience, performance, uncertainty, and distributional indicators with prior knowledge and alternative explanations (e.g., data quality changes).

Model recalibration or adaptation is triggered through composite gating mechanisms, implemented either as Boolean rules (requiring concurrent exceedance across multiple metric families) or as score-based aggregation into a unified drift risk index. w:r.w:delText: Physics simulations are the most expensive component. A single PFLOTRAN run for a 2D cross-section case takes minutes; a full 3D site model may take hours or days. but still benefit from parallel execution. Surrogate training requires GPU resources for efficient execution. Initial training of a U-FNO or U-Net model may take hours on a modern GPU. Training, update, inference, and uncertainty-processing times must be benchmarked on specified hardware; the current adaptive-replay evidence does not supply an end-to-end cost comparison.

Inference and diagnostic calculations may be less costly than physics simulations, but their operational cost depends on model size, monitoring frequency, ensemble size, and data volume. Resource planning should use measured throughput and include uncertainty-processing and data-transfer costs.

The architecture should not assume that all components run on the same hardware. Physics simulations may run on one HPC system, training on another, and monitoring on a third. Data must flow between these environments reliably, with appropriate handling of different file systems, network configurations, and security boundaries.
Simulator coupling presents a practical challenge because physics simulators were not designed with

workflows in mind. The framework must work with simulators as they are, typically through file-based interfaces: generate input files according to simulator specifications, run the simulator as a subprocess or batch job, and parse output files to extract results. This approach is less elegant than API-based coupling but far more practical given the diversity of simulators in use across EM sites. Reproducibility requires that every result can be regenerated from archived inputs. This means versioning not just code but also training data, model weights, configuration files, and random seeds. The data management layer must support this requirement without imposing excessive overhead on routine operations. Every prediction should be traceable to the specific surrogate version, training data, and configuration that produced it.

DOE quality assurance requirements apply to software used in decision support for environmental management. These requirements do not dictate specific technologies but do constrain how the software is developed and operated. The architecture should make compliance straightforward rather than burdensome.

Configuration control requires that every deployed component has a defined version, that changes be documented and reviewed before deployment, and that the system be able to report exactly what software versions produced a given result. This applies to surrogate models, monitoring algorithms, and the framework software itself.

Verification and validation require that each component be tested against defined acceptance criteria before deployment, with test results documented and retained. For surrogate models, this means validation against properly held-out data and comparison to physics model predictions. For software components, this means unit tests, integration tests, and documented test coverage.
Traceability requires that audit logs record what data was used, what computations were performed, and what results were produced. These logs must be retained for the project lifetime
potentially decades for long-term remediation sites. The data management layer must support efficient storage and retrieval of audit information.

Corrective action procedures must define how problems are diagnosed, how fixes are implemented, and how effectiveness is verified. When a surrogate fails validation or produces unexpected results, the system must support root cause analysis and documented resolution.

w:r.w:t: The baseline comparison supplies an offline analogue of the evidence that MONITOR would collect during operations. In manuscript Figure 4, historical root mean square error (RMSE) is 0.58 µg/L and rare-regime RMSE is 10.04 µg/L. The rare-regime result is approximately 17.3 times the historical value. Reported rare plume-mass error is 32.30%, peak-concentration error is 14.20%, and Mass90 error is 7.11%. These results identify a substantial reliability difference between the two selected response regimes.

The plume metrics make the maintenance problem relevant to groundwater interpretation: concentration-field error is accompanied by discrepancies in predicted mass, peak concentration, and plume footprint. Those discrepancies motivate a review of the surrogate's applicability. They do not establish errors at actual compliance wells or demonstrate a measured change in remedy performance.

Operational MONITOR would instead produce ordered prediction–observation comparisons and uncertainty diagnostics as new observations become available. The reported aggregates do not provide that record, trajectory-level error distributions, repeat-run variability, or a verified untouched test partition. They justify investigating the high-change regime while leaving uncertainty around the reported averages unquantified.

The study selects regimes using the relative change in the number of grid cells needed to contain 90% of reference plume mass between consecutive states. Manuscript Figure 1 gives a 40th-percentile cutoff of 0.133 for historical cases and a 97th-percentile cutoff of 0.329 for rare cases. Their ratio is approximately 2.47. The bottom 40% and top 3% of the response-score distribution therefore define the historical and rare subsets used in the update comparison.

This Mass90 change score is a retrospective response descriptor. It requires the reference plume at t + 1 and cannot supply a prospective warning before that state is available. Because it counts cells rather than tracking their locations, it can also miss translation or rearrangement that leaves the footprint size unchanged. Selection by this score does not establish whether the underlying cause was a pumping change, a source change, or another operational or hydrogeological process.

The evidence supports a controlled stress condition for DETECT. It does not provide sensitivity, specificity, false-alarm frequency, or warning lead time. The framework's additional diagnostics—rolling residual variance, lag-1 autocorrelation, skewness and kurtosis, uncertainty inflation, input-distribution distances, and latent-space indicators—remain candidates for prospective testing. The available short sequence and aggregate results cannot substantiate the illustrative 60–90-day persistence rule. Future detector evaluation must use ordered trajectories, known change conditions, thresholds fixed before evaluation, and a documented time axis.

DECIDE translates the reliability concern into an explicit requirement for an update. An acceptable candidate must improve performance in the regime under review while retaining enough historical accuracy for its intended use. The adaptive-replay study presents several illustrative acceptance examples rather than one approved, preregistered deployment contract.

Table 9 and Figure 8 reproduce the four displayed controller outcomes under those two conditions. These percentages belong to that controller comparison and are not recomputed from the separate manuscript Figure 4 RMSE values.

Threshold adaptive forgetting clears the historical limit by 3.5 percentage points and the rare-improvement target by 0.8 points. Loss-balanced replay clears them by 8.9 and 0.5 points. The small rare-improvement margins make repeated-run and independent-test evaluation consequential. Fixed replay and loss-balanced replay with a floor fail the historical condition despite exceeding the rare-improvement target.

The defensible decision is controller-specific: retain the threshold-adaptive and loss-balanced outcomes as candidates for further evaluation under this illustrative screen. Final acceptance requires a frozen performance contract, common evaluation partitions, documented metric definitions, and uncertainty assessment. No blanket acceptance of adaptive replay follows from these four points.

The study prepares rare update cases from the top 3% response regime and historical replay cases from the bottom 40%. Rare cases supply the behavior to be learned, and historical examples constrain forgetting. This provides a controlled dataset for comparing update strategies.

The framework's approximately 70–75% historical-replay guidance is a design starting point. It is not a measured batch composition for every experiment. The controller comparison includes a plotted run that reaches a replay cap of r = 0.8; verifying its actual historical/new exposure requires the executed sampling definition, batch counts, and controller logs.

Fixed replay therefore provides a more favorable RMSE balance than simple fine-tuning or EWC within this particular comparison; it does not remove the retention cost.

Manuscript Figure 3 separately reports a full-network historical/rare RMSE pair of 0.64/0.99 µg/L, compared with 1.11/3.92 µg/L for decoder-only fine-tuning. Likewise, the 80.4% fixed-replay historical degradation and 88.9% rare improvement displayed in the controller comparison differ from the 77.6% and 87.9% calculated from Table 10. These differences require panel-specific denominators, splits, and exposure records; rounding alone should not be assumed to explain them.

The displayed adaptive trajectory reaches r = 0.8 for most of its 100 plotted epochs. This demonstrates selection of a high replay ratio in that run, but it does not isolate the effect of adaptive scheduling. A fixed-ratio-0.8 comparison with matched initialization, random seeds, update budget, and historical exposure is needed to determine whether adaptation itself provides additional benefit.

Point-prediction improvement does not establish that a candidate expresses uncertainty reliably. CALIBRATE requires independent calibration data, a specified interval procedure, and reporting of empirical coverage, interval width, and reliability across relevant regimes and locations. The framework uses coverage near a nominal 90% level as an illustrative objective; the applicable coverage tolerance and acceptable width must be set for the intended decision.

The adaptive-replay study provides no prediction intervals, ensemble or dropout samples, conformal calibration residuals, calibration parameters, or reliability diagrams. Consequently, the candidate outcomes that pass the Figure 8 screen remain awaiting calibration. A deterministic surrogate could use residual-based conformal calibration if suitable independent data exist. Its usual marginal-coverage guarantees require the relevant exchangeability assumptions and cannot be presumed under distribution shift or within temporally dependent trajectories.

The next evidence package should keep controller-selection data, uncertainty-calibration data, and untouched final-test trajectories distinct. It should report coverage and width separately for historical and rare regimes and at decision-relevant locations. Those requirements establish the next experiment; no numerical calibration result can be inferred from the RMSE reductions already reported.
DEPLOY: final validation and promotion decision

DEPLOY requires an untouched final test and a versioned acceptance record. Evaluation must address the frozen historical/rare performance contract, priority-location error limits, uncertainty coverage and width, spatial and temporal consistency, and systematic bias near decision boundaries. The record must identify the model, preprocessing, training and calibration configurations, data provenance, reviewer, and promotion decision.

Those promotion artifacts are not available for the adaptive-replay study. The case-study outcome is therefore a documented hold for calibration and final validation, with no demonstrated deployment. Candidate rejection does not authorize use of an invalid incumbent: if operational validity is in question, the withdrawal and governed retraining policy in Section 3.1.5 applies. The offline screening results in this case study are not themselves an operational rollback event.

The seven steps form a connected decision argument. Baseline evaluation identifies a high-change response regime with poor predictions. Retrospective detection labels the stress condition. DECIDE specifies the adaptation–retention tradeoff; PREPARE supplies rare cases and historical replay; UPDATE produces quantitative candidate comparisons. The two controller outcomes that pass the illustrative screen then encounter the unfulfilled calibration and final-validation requirements. The contribution is a controlled update case study placed within an auditable lifecycle. The available results show that rare-regime recovery and historical retention must be evaluated jointly. They also show why an update that improves point predictions remains a candidate until uncertainty, independence, and governance requirements are met.

The next increment should first resolve the dataset time axis and trajectory split, archive executed configurations and predictions, and reconcile the figure-specific comparisons. It should then freeze the detector and acceptance rules, compare adaptive scheduling with a matched fixed-replay control, calibrate uncertainty independently, and evaluate an untouched final test. Efficiency should be assessed separately from accuracy. The earlier report's order-of-magnitude speedup expectations and 6–10 targeted-simulation starting point remain context and design guidance, not measured benefits of this controller. w:r.w:delText: The surrogate model literature review was conducted using Web of Science with search terms targeting
applications in groundwater modeling, subsurface flow prediction, and contaminant transport simulation. The search covered publications from 2018 to 2024, reflecting the rapid development of

methods for scientific computing during this period. Papers were selected based on relevance to groundwater remediation applications, with emphasis on architectures that have demonstrated success in predicting spatiotemporal fields from physics-based model outputs.

The review identified six primary architectural families with demonstrated applicability to subsurface modeling: convolutional encoder-decoder models, operator-learning models, sequence models, generative models, regression and classical surrogates, and structured domain surrogates. Each family offers distinct advantages depending on the prediction task, data availability, and computational constraints. Comprehensive reviews by Razavi et al. (2012) and Asher et al. (2015) provide foundational context for surrogate modeling in water resources applications. Surrogate modeling publication trends were quantified using the Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate Analytics). We performed a topic search (12/5/2025) combining groundwater and subsurface keywords with surrogate-modeling terms (TS = ((groundwater OR subsurface OR aquifer OR
)), limited to articles and reviews in English for the period 2005 to 2026.
